claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state with uniform elemental distribution.
The metastable solid solution decomposes through grain-boundary-mediated, diffusion-controlled precipitation.
The precipitating phases are Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Intermetallic precipitation preferentially nucleates at grain boundaries.
Early-stage precipitates are discrete nanoscale particles.
Early-stage precipitates promote formation or integrity of a continuous protective oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale preserves high-temperature oxidation resistance during short exposures.
Prolonged thermal exposure causes the Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates to coarsen.
Prolonged exposure causes the precipitates to form an interconnected intermetallic network.
An interconnected intermetallic network creates local electrochemical potential differences and galvanic sites.
The galvanic sites accelerate localized corrosion.
Grain-boundary intermetallic precipitation alters the local alloy chemistry.
Short heat-treatment durations cause only a minor compromise in corrosion resistance.
Prolonged exposure significantly degrades corrosion resistance relative to the as-quenched state.
High-temperature oxidation resistance may remain adequate after prolonged exposure despite degraded corrosion resistance.
The as-quenched baseline is single-phase and contains no significant intermetallic precipitation.
The as-quenched baseline exhibits homogeneous corrosion and oxidation behavior.
The proposed precipitation and coarsening transitions occur within a service-relevant temperature range of 500–700°C.
